# The own-depth capacity theorem for three consecutive interval fibers

This proves a bounded special case of the own-depth capacity proposal. It
does not infer the general capacity statement from concavity; that generic
statement is disproved in `candidate de5fcdadbcbc6e59`.

## 1. Statement and normalization

Let K_0,K_1,K_2 be positive-length compact intervals in R, with

    (K_0+K_2)/2 subset K_1.

At the three integer indices define g(z,x) as the unnormalized own-interval
depth, namely the smaller distance from x to its two endpoints. Put
A_z=max g(z,.)=|K_z|/2. For a closed ambient halfspace H in R^2 define

    nu(H)=sum_(z=0)^2 sup_(x in K_z, (z,x) in H) g(z,x),

where an empty fiber intersection contributes zero. Then a point of one
of these fibers has every containing halfspace of capacity at least

    T=(A_0+A_1+A_2)/2.                                   (1)

An affine shear in the continuous coordinate can make both endpoint
midpoints zero. Write the resulting intervals as

    K_0=[-A_0,A_0], K_2=[-A_2,A_2], K_1=[-L,U].

With s=A_0+A_2 and m=min(A_0,A_2), compatibility says L,U>=s/2, and
A_1=(L+U)/2. This shear translates each fiber without changing own-depth
values or ambient halfspaces. A common reflection can make L<=U.

If any A_z>=T, its own midpoint already has capacity at least T from
that fiber alone. In the remaining nonheavy case all three A_z<T.
The point constructed below lies in the middle fiber.

## 2. Exact endpoint allocation lemma

For positive a,b, let r_0+r_2=2x be two real thresholds. The minimum of

    min(a,(a-r_0)_+) + min(b,(b-r_2)_+)

over these thresholds is exactly

    min(min(a,b),(a+b-2x)_+).                             (2)

If either summand is saturated at its full value, the sum is at least
min(a,b). If neither is full, their sum is at least (a+b-2x)_+ by
the elementary positive-part inequality. This proves the lower bound.
The value min(a,b) is attained by making that smaller summand full and
the other zero, using sufficiently separated thresholds. If the proposed
value a+b-2x is between zero and min(a,b), distribute that value as
nonnegative residuals no larger than a,b and put r_i=A_i-residual_i.
Both summands are then unsaturated with the required threshold sum.
If a+b-2x<=0, take both thresholds at least their interval lengths.
This proves all cases, including equality at the saturation thresholds.

The upper half of an endpoint interval is [0,A_z], so its up-cap capacity
is exactly the length of this halfinterval above the cap threshold.
A line through (1,x) has endpoint thresholds x-a and x+a. Equation (2)
therefore gives the exact minimum total endpoint up-cap capacity

    min(m,(s-2x)_+).

For down-caps the same calculation gives min(m,(s+2x)_+). Consequently
the minima over all nonvertical up- and down-caps through (1,x) are

    Ucap(x)=min(A_1,U-x)+min(m,(s-2x)_+),
    Lcap(x)=min(A_1,L+x)+min(m,(s+2x)_+),                 (3)

for -L<=x<=U. Formula (3) keeps all oblique slopes and their possible
large-slope saturation; it does not restrict the cuts to horizontal ones.

## 3. An explicit capacity center

Assume the nonheavy case and L<=U, and define

    x_*=max(0,T-m-L).                                    (4)

The nonheavy endpoint condition gives

    A_1>s-2m,

while the nonheavy middle condition gives A_1<s. Hence

    T-m<A_1,       0<T-A_1=(s-A_1)/2<m.                 (5)

Put c=(U-L)/2, the middle midpoint. Since L+c=A_1 and T-m<A_1,
equation (4) gives x_*<=c. Also L>=s/2 implies

    T-m-L <= T-s/2-m=A_1/2-m <= T/2,

where the last inequality follows from A_1<s (and m>0). Thus

    0<=x_*<=min(c,T/2).                                  (6)

The point belongs to K_1. Since x_*>=T-m-L, (5) and the down-cap
formula in (3) give

    Lcap(x_*)=min(A_1,L+x_*)+m>=T.

For up-caps, x_*<=c makes the own-fiber term equal A_1. Equation (6)
gives s-2x_*>=s-T=T-A_1>0, and (5) gives m>T-A_1. Therefore

    Ucap(x_*)>=A_1+(T-A_1)=T.

A vertical halfspace through the middle index contains either fibers
0 and 1 or fibers 1 and 2 (or all three). Its capacity is at least
A_1+m>T by (5). Every containing halfspace can be shifted to pass
through the candidate without increasing capacity. This proves (1)
for every closed ambient halfspace.

The construction uses one deterministic point of an actual fiber. It
does not claim a comparable formula for more than three fibers or for
unequally spaced three-point bases.

## 4. Computational diagnostic beyond the proved case

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/own_interval_capacity_search.py` screens the two halfinterval measures
directly. It found no failure in 9,600 sampled compatible integer sequences
with 3 through 10 positive interval fibers. Its slope minima are evaluated
at all halfinterval endpoint events and at infinite-slope limits. This
observation supplies no proof beyond Sections 1--3; it is recorded only
to distinguish the tested special structure from the false generic
concave-function capacity claim.
